title: Private Deployments \n\nCustomer Requirements, Reference Architectures, On-Prem Packaging, Day-2 Ops, Upgrade & Rollback Guide
author: Emily Zhang
content:
Overview

Purpose
This guide consolidates customer-facing requirements, recommended reference architectures, on-prem packaging options, and day-2 operational runbooks for Redwood Inference private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It is intended for solutions engineers, SREs, and customers' infrastructure teams preparing for a private deployment.

Scope
- VPC-based private deployments (cloud-managed private control plane)
- Air-gapped / on-prem package deployments
- Reference architectures for small, medium, and large footprints
- Day-2 operations, monitoring, SLOs, and common runbooks
- Upgrade and rollback procedures and preflight checks
- Customer requirements checklist used during discovery and onboarding

Summary of recommended approach
- Use the reference architecture that most closely matches the customer's workload profile (latency-sensitive vs throughput-oriented).
- Validate network, security, and compliance requirements during discovery and include them in the customer requirements document that is signed off before provisioning.
- For production traffic, run a staged canary upgrade with automated health checks and a documented rollback path.

1) Customer requirements library (discovery checklist)
Below is a standard checklist used during pre-sales and onboarding to capture environment constraints and requirements. Capture answers in the onboarding ticket and attach network diagrams and ACLs.

| Category | Required info / Example values | Acceptable values / Notes | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Deployment mode | VPC (AWS / GCP / Azure) or On-Prem air-gapped | cloud-vpc / onprem-airgapped | customer infra 
| Contact & approvals | Primary infra contact, security approver, legal | list of emails + SLA sign-off | customer PM
| Network & DNS | CIDR blocks, outbound proxy, DNS for control-plane endpoints | /16 recommended for full cluster; provide NAT/IGW details | customer infra
| Subnet requirements | Public load-balancer subnet + private worker subnets | At least 3 AZs for HA on cloud | customer infra
| Egress controls | S3 endpoints, KMS endpoints, allowed IP ranges | VPC endpoints recommended; whitelist Redwood control-plane IPs | customer security
| IP allowlist | IPs for support, CI/CD, partner integrations | CIDR list | customer security
| Hardware profile | GPU type(s), number nodes, expected throughput | e.g., 4x A10G or 8x A100-80GB | customer infra
| Storage needs | Type (NVMe / EBS), capacity, IOPS | Persistent volumes for model cache; object storage for artifacts | customer infra
| Compliance & encryption | KMS/HSM, audit logging, log retention | Bring-your-own-KMS: required? | legal/security
| Monitoring & metrics | Existing metrics stack (Prometheus/Grafana/Datadog) | Must allow metric scraping or remote write | customer infra
| Backup & restores | Snapshot frequency, RTO/RPO expectations | Daily snapshots; RTO <= 4 hrs recommended for control-plane | customer infra

Note: Collect topology diagrams (VPC peering, transit gateways, firewall rules) as part of requirements.

2) Reference architectures (high-level)
Use the brief architectures below to align expectations. Each architecture includes control plane, data plane, and optional private upload/ingestion endpoints.

Small (POC / low throughput)
- 1 control-plane node (VM), 1-2 worker nodes (GPUs), single AZ (non-HA)
- Use small model variants or quantized profiles for cost control
- Suitable for functional testing and onboarding

Medium (production, moderate throughput)
- Control plane HA (3 masters across AZs), 3-6 worker nodes across 3 AZs
- Load balancer in front of inference API; autoscaler enabled for worker pool
- Dedicated Redis/KV cache and object store (S3-compatible)

Large (high throughput / enterprise)
- Multi-region or multi-cluster deployment for geographic redundancy
- Dedicated GPU node pools per workload type (batch vs low-latency)
- Ingress routing by customer route policy, private peering to backends

Topology and networking recommendations
- Subnet sizing: allocate for control-plane, worker nodes, and management (SSH, bastion)
- Use internal load balancers for inference endpoints and public load balancers for customer-facing control plane dashboards (if required)
- VPC endpoints for object storage and KMS recommended to avoid public egress

3) On-prem packaging & installation options
Supported packaging formats
- Helm chart: recommended for customers running Kubernetes (k8s v1.24+). Values.yaml templates provided for common footprints.
- Air-gapped tarball + installer: for fully isolated environments. Installer supports offline image import and local registry.
- VM bundle: prebuilt VM images for customers that don't run Kubernetes.

Minimum supported platform requirements (on-prem)
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (preferred) or RHEL 8.6+
- Container runtime: containerd 1.6+ or Docker 20.10+ (only for VM bundle)
- Kubernetes: v1.24+ (for helm deployment)
- GPU drivers: NVIDIA driver 535+ and CUDA 11.8+ (match vendor matrix)
- Storage: NVMe local for model caching recommended; 1TB baseline per node for medium workloads
- Network: 1Gbps minimum per node; 10Gbps recommended for multi-GPU nodes

Packaging checksums and verification
- All packages include SHA256 checksums and signed manifests. During air-gapped installs the installer will verify signatures against the customer's provided public key.

4) Day-2 operations (monitoring, runbooks, SLOs)
Monitoring stack and integrations
- Metrics: export Prometheus metrics, with recommended scrape intervals for GPU metrics (15s)
- Logs: structured JSON logs shipped to customer's ELK/Datadog; include request_id and model metadata
- Traces: optional OpenTelemetry export for per-request latency breakdowns

SLOs and alert thresholds (baseline recommendation)
- Availability: 99.9% (monthly) for production inference endpoints
- Error rate: p99 < 0.1% request errors (5xx)
- Latency: p50 < 50ms (small models), p95 < 200ms, p99 < 500ms (adjust by model size)
- GPU queueing latency: alert when average queue time > 200ms for more than 5m

Suggested alert definitions
- node.gpu.utilization > 95% for > 10m -> action: scale worker pool or add capacity
- http.request.5xx.rate > 0.5% over 5m -> investigate runtime errors and model regressions
- kv-cache.miss.rate increase > 30% -> investigate cache eviction or model changes

Day-2 runbooks (examples)
1. Scaling up worker pool (manual)
   a. Verify current utilization: promql: avg(node_gpu_utilization{role="worker"}) by (pool)
   b. Increase desired replicas in autoscaler or run: kubectl scale deployment inference-workers --replicas=8
   c. Confirm new nodes join, wait for GPU drivers to be healthy, and sanity-check model inference on new nodes
2. Mitigating high latency (queueing)
   a. Identify which model and route has higher queue time (trace + metrics)
   b. If model is large, switch traffic to a smaller variant or enable prefix caching for the workload
   c. If resource-starved, scale worker pool or move traffic to dedicated node pool
3. Handling 5xx error spikes
   a. Check runtime logs for OOM or kernel panics
   b. If caused by bad model or update, rollback the model or route to previous stable version

5) Upgrade and rollback procedures
Principles
- Prefer staged canary rollouts with automated health checks at each phase
- Always run preflight checks and collect baseline metrics before an upgrade
- Maintain automated backups of persistent state (control-plane DB, config) before changes

Preflight checklist
1. Verify backup snapshot exists and restore test passed in staging in last 30 days
2. Confirm health of control-plane (all masters Ready) and worker pools (nodeReady and GPUReady)
3. Ensure no long-running jobs or model migrations are in progress
4. Verify that Prometheus alerts are green and that alerting channels are acknowledged

Staged upgrade (example for Helm/K8s deployment)
1. Upgrade canary subset: helm upgrade inference --set global.canary=true --namespace redwood --wait --timeout 10m
2. Run automated canary health checks for 15-30 minutes: increase in error rate < 0.1% and p95 latency regression < 10%
3. If canary passes, progressively upgrade remaining replicas with rolling update strategy
4. Post-upgrade validation: run synthetic load test and verify metrics against baseline for 60 minutes

Rollback steps (if canary fails or post-upgrade regressions)
1. Immediately halt rollout and set traffic split back to stable: kubectl patch svc inference --patch '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"inference-stable"}}}'
2. Rollback Helm release: helm rollback inference <previous-release> --namespace redwood
3. If control-plane change caused data migration, run documented migration rollback (contact internal DB owners if needed)
4. Open incident with oncall SRE and attach metrics and logs for RCA

6) Validation & acceptance tests
Minimum acceptance tests to run after deployment/upgrade:
- Smoke test: single inference request to each model type with expected token output
- Load test: ramp to N RPS for 5 minutes validating latency SLOs (N depends on customer expected throughput)
- Failover test: simulate single-AZ outage and validate HA behaviour for control-plane (medium/large topologies)
- Security test: verify KMS access, audit logs are generated, and S3 access via VPC endpoints works

7) Ownership, contact points, and escalation paths
- Deployment owner: eng-private-deployments team (primary: Solutions Engineering)
- Oncall escalation: eng-sre -> primary oncall -> secondary oncall (see oncall roster)
- Support contact for enterprise customers: customer-success enterprise lead (add to ticket when provisioning)

8) Appendices
A. Example Helm values snippet (small footprint)
```yaml
replicaCount: 2
worker:
  gpu: A10G
  resources:
    limits:
      cpu: "16"
      memory: "64Gi"
  nodeSelector:
    workload: inference
global:
  canary: false
  registry: "registry.redwood-inference.local"
```

B. Example rollback commands
- kube: helm rollback inference <release> --namespace redwood
- service switch (if using split service): kubectl patch svc inference --patch '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"inference-stable"}}}'

C. Useful queries (Prometheus examples)
- GPU utilization: avg(node_gpu_utilization{role="worker"})
- Request error rate: sum(increase(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(increase(http_requests_total[5m]))

Document maintenance and ownership
This page is owned by eng-private-deployments. Updates to packaging, supported OS, and driver versions must be coordinated with eng-infra and eng-serving-runtime. Major changes require review from security-and-compliance and eng-sre.
